documentNotes.title: General note
documentNotes.statement:
**General note.** Maybe not all problems have correct questions. Some questions (maybe the main question of the problem, maybe one of the subquestions) may make no real sense. In this case you have to write in your answer (in English or Russian): «**impossible situation – ситуация невозможна**». Of course, this answer has to be explained numerically or logically.

**Data from the tables** (Planetary data, stars, constants, etc.) may be used for solving every problem.

The answers «**Да-Yes**» or «**Нет-No**» have to be written in English or Russian.

problems.title: Dreams of the Polar Bear
problems.statement: Terrestrial Polar Bear-observer, watching the lunar disk in the phase of the full moon, in his dreams became thousand times closer to it. What did the magnitude of the Moon become? The solution has to include an artistic picture with an image of the Bear-observer on the North Pole.

solution.statement: **Official sketches for solutions.** The source notes that these sketches are not full; team leaders should give more detailed explanations, while correct student solutions sufficient for 8 points may be shorter.

sections.title: Solution
sections.statement:
It would seem that approaching 10 times closer to an object reduces its apparent magnitude by 5 magnitudes, and so approaching $1000=10^3$ times closer reduces the apparent magnitude by $3\cdot5=15$ magnitudes. The magnitude of the Moon would be equal to $-12.7-15=-27.7$?

Would it? It turns out that in this case the Moon shines 2.3 times brighter than the Sun! In fact, this cannot happen!

Actually, the rule of reducing the magnitude by 5 when approaching the object 10 times closer is valid only for point-like objects, or objects for which the small-angle approximation is acceptable, i.e., an approach 10 times closer to the object increases the apparent solid angle by a factor of 100. Indeed, the magnitude decrease of extended objects, like the lunar disc, is related to the increase of the object’s apparent solid angle while keeping brightness unchanged.

The solid angle of the visible surface of the Moon from the Earth is

$$\Omega_1=\pi(4.6\cdot10^{-3}\ \mathrm{rad})^2\approx6.7\cdot10^{-5}\ \mathrm{rad}^2.$$

When using the small-angle approximation, approaching $10^3$ times closer would increase the visible area by the factor of $10^6$ times, and it would become 67 rad². However, this solid angle cannot be larger than the solid angle of a hemisphere, $2\pi\ \mathrm{rad}^2=6.3\ \mathrm{rad}^2$. That is, in the calculations we have overestimated the area by a factor of at least $67/6.3=10.6$, and make an error in the magnitude of at least $2.5\log(10.6)=2.6$. Thus, the magnitude of the lunar disk cannot be less than $-27.7+2.6=-25.1$.

More precise calculations show that when approaching 1000 times closer to the surface of the Moon (approximately from 380 thousand km to 380 km), the apparent solid angle will be

$$\Omega_2=2\pi\left(1-\cos\left[\arcsin\frac{R_M}{R_M+h}\right]\right)\ \mathrm{rad}^2\approx2\pi\left(1-\cos\left[\arcsin\frac{1.74}{2.12}\right]\right)\ \mathrm{rad}^2\approx2.7\ \mathrm{rad}^2,$$

i.e. it will increase by a factor of approximately $\Omega_2/\Omega_1=40000$ and (in this model of the same brightness of the lunar surface) the magnitude is

$$-12.7-2.5\log(40000)\approx-24.2.$$

sections.title: Official grading criteria
sections.statement:
Solution: 7 pt in total, including:
- Understanding about impossibility to use approximation of point-like objects — 3 pt.
- Result approximately Ω₂/Ω₁=40000 — 2 pt.
- Formula and final calculations −12.7−2.5log(40000)≈−24.2 — 2 pt.

For any solution based on calculations in approximation of point-like objects or any answer resulting in larger than the Sun brightness, total mark (except mark for the picture) should not be larger than 1 pt for group α or 0.5 pt for group β.

Artistic picture of the Bear — 1 pt.

*Jury note: evaluate the solution in essence rather than formal presence of sentences/formulae; award points when subsequent steps de facto use the required positions.*

problems.title: Great oppositions
problems.statement: Now great oppositions of Mars happen every 15 or 17 years. To simplify colonization of Mars, to improve environmental conditions on it, and to increase the effect of the great oppositions, our civilization has conceived an ambitious project: to reduce by 6.0% the semi-major axis of this planet’s orbit, while keeping the eccentricity of the orbit unchanged. How often will the great oppositions of Mars occur in the case of the new orbit?

solution.statement: **Official sketches for solutions.** The source notes that these sketches are not full; team leaders should give more detailed explanations, while correct student solutions sufficient for 8 points may be shorter.

sections.title: Solution
sections.statement:
Reducing the by 6.0% the semi-major axis of Mars orbit changes its sidereal period:

$$(T_1/T_0)^2=(A_1/A_0)^3,$$

$$T_1=T_0(A_1/A_0)^{3/2}=1.880\ \mathrm{years}\cdot(0.94)^{3/2}=1.713\ \mathrm{years}.$$

Syndical period $T_{1S}$ of new Mars may be found from formula

$$1/T_{1S}=1/T_E-1/T_1,\qquad T_{1S}=T_1T_E/(T_1-T_E)=2.402\ \mathrm{years}.$$

That is, oppositions of Mars (of any kind) will occur every 2.402 years. After 5 such cycles, the Earth and Mars return approximately to the same positions. It is the new period for repeating the great oppositions. Answer is “every 12 years”.

*Note: Inaccurate data calculations (of $T_1$, for example) in this problem can easily lead to incorrect results. In calculating the synodic motion of Mars the exact value of the fractional part of the period is very important.*

sections.title: Official grading criteria
sections.statement:
- Correct using Kepler’s III law and finding T₁=T₀(A₁/A₀)³ᐟ²=1.713 years — 3 pt.
- Correct finding synodic period ~2.4 years — 2 pt.
- Understanding that the great opposition is one of five, and result 12 years — 3 pt.

*Jury note: evaluate the solution in essence rather than formal presence of sentences/formulae; award points when subsequent steps de facto use the required positions.*

problems.title: Proxima Centauri
problems.statement: Can the star Proxima Centauri be visible from the vicinity of Alpha Centauri by naked eye? (**«да-yes»** or **«нет-no»**). Justify your solution by calculations of the corresponding apparent magnitude of Proxima Centauri.

solution.statement: **Official sketches for solutions.** The source notes that these sketches are not full; team leaders should give more detailed explanations, while correct student solutions sufficient for 8 points may be shorter.

sections.title: Solution
sections.statement:
Let us find the distance $d$ between Proxima and Alpha Centauri.

$$d=(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{1/2},$$

where x, y and z are projections of the distance on the axes of our coordinate system. Necessary data we should take from the “Data on some stars”. Approximately

$$x=|\alpha_{\rm PC}-\alpha_{\alpha C}|\cos\delta_{P\alpha C}\,L_{P\alpha C}=\frac{|\alpha_{\rm PC}-\alpha_{\alpha C}|\cos\delta_{P\alpha C}}{p_{P\alpha C}},$$

$$y=|\delta_{\rm PC}-\delta_{\alpha C}|L_{P\alpha C}=\frac{|\delta_{\rm PC}-\delta_{\alpha C}|}{p_{P\alpha C}},$$

$$z=|L_{\rm PC}-L_{\alpha C}|=|1/p_{\rm PC}-1/p_{\alpha C}|,$$

where $\alpha,\delta,L,p$ are right ascension, declination, distance from the Earth, parallax, and values with sub-index PC are related to Proxima Centauri; those with sub-index αC, to Alpha Centauri; and PαC, to the middle point of Proxima and Alpha Centauri. So, from the “Data on some stars”, we should take $\alpha,\delta,p$ of Proxima and Alpha Centauri. Calculations give us:

$$x=0.0269\ \mathrm{pc},\quad y=0.0425\ \mathrm{pc},\quad z=0.0383\ \mathrm{pc},\quad d=0.0632\ \mathrm{pc}.$$

Thus, in comparison with observation from the Earth, the magnitude of Proxima Centauri while observed from the vicinity of Alpha Centauri is smaller by

$$\Delta m=5\log(L_{P\alpha C}/d)=-5\log(d\,p_{P\alpha C})\approx6.57$$

than the magnitude while observed from the Earth.

$$m=m_E-\Delta m=11.05-6.57\approx4.5.$$

It is less than the limit value for naked eye, 6, so Proxima Centauri can be visible from the vicinity of Alpha Centauri by naked eye, «да-yes».

*Note: To prove the proposal «нет-no» of the first question, it would not be necessary to make so many calculations of x, y, z and d. It is evident that $d\ge z$, so if Proxima Centauri cannot be visible from the distance z, it would be also not visible from the distance d.*

sections.title: Official grading criteria
sections.statement:
- Understanding to use formula d=(x²+y²+z²)¹ᐟ² — 1 pt.
- Correct formulae for x,y,z — 3×1 pt.
- Correct final calculation of d — 1 pt.
- Correct comparing with the magnitude as seen from Earth and result of magnitude from α Cen — 1.5 pt.
- Final comparing with 6 magnitudes and answer «да-yes» — 1.5 pt.

*Jury note: evaluate the solution in essence rather than formal presence of sentences/formulae; award points when subsequent steps de facto use the required positions.*

problems.title: Hydroplanet
problems.statement: Hydroplanet consists of a rocky “core” of radius $\boldsymbol{R}$ and a thick layer of water surrounding it from all sides. Local humans live at the bottom of this world’s ocean (i.e., on the surface of the “core”), and hydrosphere is an analogue of our atmosphere for them. Local scientists observe astronomical objects from the bottom of the ocean. Like on our Earth, the duration of day-night period on Hydroplanet is T = 24 hours.

parts.statement: Find the minimum depth $\boldsymbol{H}$ of the ocean, for which celestial bodies will be visible at the horizon.
What will be the duration of the day for inhabitants of the planet’s equator? The disk of the central star can be considered as a point source of light.

Calculate the value of “atmoshperical” refraction at the horizon on such a planet.

Points of your solution have to include drawings with all necessary sizes or angular sizes. The outer surface of the ocean is smooth, no waves or ripples.

problems.statementAfterParts: Points of your solution have to include drawings with all necessary sizes or angular sizes. The outer surface of the ocean is smooth, no waves or ripples.

solution.statement: **Official sketches for solutions.** The source notes that these sketches are not full; team leaders should give more detailed explanations, while correct student solutions sufficient for 8 points may be shorter.

sections.title: Solution
sections.statement:
When passing the border between the airless space and water, rays are reflected:

$$\sin\alpha=n\sin\beta.$$

As a result the rays go steeper after refraction. Due to the total reflection effect, only those rays reach observers at the outer surface of the ocean, which are directed, in the water medium, so that their angle with respect to the normal to the water surface is below the critical value that occurs for $\sin\alpha=1$, i.e. for $\alpha=90^{\circ}$.

$$1=n\sin\beta,\qquad\beta=\arcsin(1/n),$$

$$\beta=\arcsin(1/1.334)=\arcsin(0.7496)=48^{\circ}33'.$$

![Official Hydroplanet refraction diagram, with R, H, β and 90°−β](#p4-hydroplanet-astra-s8-r2)

For low depth of the ocean, this is the largest zenith distance from which rays reach observers. When increasing the ocean’s depth, this critical zenith angle increases because of the surface curvature. Drawing a plot, it is easy to find that light from the horizon line begins to come in the case of the minimal ocean depth that satisfies the condition:

$$\sin\beta=R/(R+H),\qquad1/n=R/(R+H),\qquad H=(n-1)R.$$

**4.1.** Answer: $H=0.334R$.

**4.2.** It appears from the same plot that the central star on the sky of the Hydroplanet passes, from its rise to its set, the angle

$$\tau=(90^{\circ}-\beta)+180^{\circ}+(90^{\circ}-\beta)=360^{\circ}-2\beta=262.12^{\circ}.$$

In hour units, this is $17^{\mathrm h}29^{\mathrm m}$.

**4.3.** It appears from the same plot that it is the angle $90^{\circ}-\beta$ that is analogous to the refraction angle at the horizon for such a planet.

$$r=90^{\circ}-\beta=41^{\circ}27'.$$

*Source note: the key prints 262.12° in 4.2; its printed β=48°33′ gives 262°54′ for 360°−2β. The printed angle and time are retained.*

figures.alt: Official Hydroplanet refraction diagram, with R, H, β and 90°−β

sections.title: Official grading criteria
sections.statement:
**Common part**
- Understanding nature of effect, total reflection effect — 2 pt.
- Correct drawing (also showing total reflection effect) — 1 pt.
- Using refractive index of water n=1.334, calculation sinβ and β — 1.5 pt.

**4.1.** Answer H=0.334R — 1.5 pt.  
**4.2.** Calculation and correct answer — 1 pt.  
**4.3.** Picture, calculation and correct answer — 1 pt.

problems.title: Climate
problems.statement:
The XXXII (32$^{\mathrm{nd}}$) century AD. Due to unknown reasons, the Sun became cooler, not changing its size, and the inclination of ecliptic to the celestial equator plane decreased to zero. Scientists proved that the problem of preserving the Earth’s climate and the annual change of seasons can be solved by a small star, negligible mass, but similar to a main-sequence star, moving in a circular orbit around the Sun. The star will revolve around the Sun as an inner planet, resulting in establishing a temperature regime on the Earth similar to the actual one at Issyk-Kul: the average winter and summer temperatures are -3 and +17 degrees respectively.

![Supplied Hertzsprung–Russell diagram with temperature, absolute magnitude and spectral class axes](#p5-hr-diagram-astra-s8-r1)

figures.alt: Supplied Hertzsprung–Russell diagram with temperature, absolute magnitude and spectral class axes

parts.statement: Estimate the temperature of the cool Sun.
Estimate to what spectral class the star which will be placed in the desired orbit will correspond.

solution.statement: **Official sketches for solutions.** The source notes that these sketches are not full; team leaders should give more detailed explanations, while correct student solutions sufficient for 8 points may be shorter.

sections.title: Solution
sections.statement:
In order to get an inner orbit of the star that would provide a seasonal cycle with a periodicity of 1 year, it is necessary that its close position with the Earth would take place once a year. That is, the synodic period of its revolution should be one year. It is not difficult to find that the sidereal period of revolution of the celestial body must be equal to

$$T=1\ \mathrm{year}\times1\ \mathrm{year}/(1\ \mathrm{year}+1\ \mathrm{year})=0.5\ \mathrm{years},$$

and the radius of its orbit, from the III Kepler’s law:

$$R=R_0(T_1/T_0)^{2/3}=0.63R_0.$$

Thus, the new celestial body will once a year become close to the Earth at a distance of $R_0-R=0.37$ au, providing summer on the planet, and once a year move away to a distance of $R_0+R=1.63$ au, leaving the Earth in winter.

The ratio of energies received by the Earth from the new star in summer and winter will be

$$\ddot E_S/\ddot E_W=(R_0+R)^2/(R_0-R)^2=19.4.$$

The ratio of these energies to the energy $\ddot E_0$, received from the new star at a distance of 1 au is

$$\ddot E_S/\ddot E_0=R_0^2/(R_0-R)^2=7.3,$$

$$\ddot E_W/\ddot E_0=R_0^2/(R_0-R)^2=0.38.$$

At the same time, the Earth will always receive additional energy $E_1$ from the cooler Sun, that is, $E_S=E_1+\ddot E_S$ in the summer, and $E_W=E_1+\ddot E_W$. To keep the heat balance, all the incoming energy should be radiated.

The ratio of the energy radiated by the Earth in summer and winter will be

$$\mathcal E_S/\mathcal E_W=T_S^4/T_W^4=(290\ \mathrm K)^4/(270\ \mathrm K)^4=1.33.$$

Neglecting the effects of delays of the seasons compared to the maxima and minima of the energy income, let us assume that $\mathcal E_S=E_S$, $\mathcal E_W=E_W$. Then we can write:

$$E_1+\ddot E_S=1.33(E_1+\ddot E_W),$$

$$E_1+19.4\ddot E_W=1.33(E_1+\ddot E_W),$$

$$(19.4-1.33)\ddot E_W=(1.33-1)E_1,$$

$$\ddot E_W/E_1=0.0183,\qquad\ddot E_S/E_1=0.355.$$

The sum of $E_1$ and the average $\ddot E$ for the period must be the same as the Earth receives nowadays, $E_0$. To estimate the average value of $\ddot E$, let us take $\ddot E_0$, and so

$$\ddot E_0/E_1=0.0486,\qquad\ddot E_0/E_0=0.0464,\qquad E_1/E_0=0.954.$$

**5.1.** Thus, the Sun in new conditions will emit 4.6% less energy, and so its temperature will be lower and equal to

$$T_1=0.954^{1/4}T_0\approx0.988T_0\approx5710\ \mathrm K.$$

**5.2.** To understand what spectral type will correspond to the star, we calculate by how many magnitudes it is fainter than the Sun:

$$\Delta M=-\frac52\lg(0.0464)\approx3.3.$$

From the HR diagram, we find that it is about the spectral type K3.

*Source note: the winter ratio is printed with (R₀−R)² in its denominator although the preceding winter distance is R₀+R and the numerical 0.38 corresponds to the latter. The printed formula is retained. Calligraphic ℰ here represents the separate radiated-energy symbol used in the key.*

sections.title: Official grading criteria
sections.statement:
- Understanding nature of effect and conclusion synodic period 1 year — 1 pt.
- Sidereal period 0.5 years — 1 pt.
- Orbital radius from Kepler’s III law — 1 pt.
- Energy balances — 2 pt.
- **5.1.** Temperature of Sun — 1 pt.
- **5.2.** ΔM=−(5/2)lg(0.0464)≈3.3 and from HR diagram spectral type K 3 — 2 pt.

*Jury note: evaluate the solution in essence rather than formal presence of sentences/formulae; award points when subsequent steps de facto use the required positions.*

problems.title: Sombrero Galaxy
problems.statement:
The Sombrero Galaxy, M104, is known as a holder of one of supermassive black holes. Images of the galaxy and its center (left side) have angular sizes 10'×7' and 10.8"×7.2" respectively. To the right, three spectra from the Hubble space telescope (in the region containing the emission lines from ionized oxygen and nitrogen) are shown for regions around the center of the galaxy. The bottom spectrum is from a region around the very center, while other two spectra are from flanking region. The values on top of the dotted lines indicate the rest (laboratory) wavelength in Ångströms.

![Sombrero Galaxy images and three spectra with wavelength scale and links to sampled regions](#p6-sombrero-astra-s8-r1)

figures.alt: Sombrero Galaxy images and three spectra with wavelength scale and links to sampled regions

parts.statement: Is M104 approaching us or receding from us? (Answer this question by sketch drawing.)
Estimate the velocity of M104 towards us or away from us.
Roughly estimate the approximate mass of the supermassive black hole in the center of M104 (answer in solar masses **m**$_{\odot}$).

solution.statement: **Official sketches for solutions.** The source notes that these sketches are not full; team leaders should give more detailed explanations, while correct student solutions sufficient for 8 points may be shorter.

sections.title: Solution
sections.statement:
**6.1.** All the lines in the spectra are shifted somewhat to longer wavelengths (redshifted). Obviously, M104 is receding from us due to the expansion of the Universe.

**6.2.** The overall receding velocity of M104 may be found from the redshift of the spectrum of the central region. Taking the average redshift of the four emission lines, we find that

$$z_{\rm av}=(\Delta\lambda/\lambda)_{\rm average}\approx0.0035,$$

and since $z\ll1$, the overall receding velocity of M104 is given by:

$$V=cz=0.0036\times300000\ \mathrm{km/s}=1050\ \mathrm{km/s}.$$

**6.3.** According to the Hubble law the distance to Sombrero Galaxy is

$$L=V/H=\frac{1050\ \mathrm{km/s}}{71\ \mathrm{km/s/Mpc}}\approx15\ \mathrm{Mpc}.$$

*Note: In reality the distance to Sombrero Galaxy is 9 Mpc. But we continue solution according to the calculated value, 15 Mpc.*

The first and second spectra have different shifts than the third one. It indicates that the gas which is generating the emission lines has a motion relative to the center of M104. The amounts of these redshifts are not too clear but evidently less than the third one. To find the mass of the smaller region near the center, we will use the first spectrum as obtained closer to the center region. The distance from the center of the galaxy to this near-center region can be found by measuring sizes at the lower picture. The angular distance is approximately 0.05 of the width of the lower image, $\alpha=0.05\times10.8''=0.54''$. To get the actual distance in a.u., it is easy to use the formula

$$R(\mathrm{a.u.})=\alpha(\mathrm{arcsec})\times L(\mathrm{pc}),$$

$$R(\mathrm{a.u.})=0.54\times15\cdot10^6\approx8\cdot10^6.$$

*Note: In reality $R(\mathrm{a.u.})=0.54\times9\cdot10^6\approx5\cdot10^6$.*

The average difference in redshifts of the first and third spectra may be estimated as about $\Delta z\approx0.0013$. Thus the velocity of the gas relative to the galactic center is about

$$V_1=c\Delta z=0.0013\times300000\ \mathrm{km/s}\approx400\ \mathrm{km/s}.$$

Then, let us assume that the gas in the region of the third spectrum revolves around the galactic center in a circular orbit with the period T. Its revolving velocity is

$$V_1=2\pi R/T=400\ \mathrm{km/s}.$$

By comparing with the average velocity of the Earth revolving around the Sun (A=1 au, P=1 year),

$$V_2=2\pi A/P=30\ \mathrm{km/s},$$

we find that

$$R/T=(V_1/V_2)(A/P)\approx13\ \mathrm{au/year}.$$

Assuming that the mass of the gas is much less than that of the galactic center and applying the Kepler’s III law (in units solar mass–au–year), we obtain the mass of the galactic center

$$M=R^3/T^2\approx13^2R\approx200\times8\cdot10^6\approx1.6\cdot10^9\quad(\mathrm{in}\ m_{\odot}).$$

*Note: In reality, we should write $M\approx200\times5\cdot10^6m_{\odot}\approx10^9m_{\odot}$.*

It is an approximation for the mass of the supermassive black hole in the center of M104.

*Source note: the key switches from z=0.0035 to 0.0036 while retaining 1050 km/s; the latter multiplication would give 1080. It also changes the moving gas from the first spectrum to the third in its prose. Both inconsistencies are retained. The “in reality” values above are statements of the 2014 source.*

sections.title: Official grading criteria
sections.statement:
- **6.1.** Spectra redshifted, receding from us — 1 pt.
- **6.2.** z_av=(Δλ/λ)_average≈0.0035 — 1 pt; V=cz=0.0036×300000 km/s=1050 km/s — 1 pt.
- **6.3.** L=V/H=1050 km/s /71 km/s/Mpc≈15 Mpc — 1 pt; R(au)=0.54×15·10⁶≈8·10⁶ — 1 pt; other correct calculations and obtaining mass of galactic center — 3 pt.

The printed 0.0036 multiplication inconsistency is retained as in the solution.

*Jury note: evaluate the solution in essence rather than formal presence of sentences/formulae; award points when subsequent steps de facto use the required positions.*
